summary.text: A 57-year-old man with hypertension, obesity class III and a prior aortic valve replacement presented to the emergency department with acute-onset chest pain, dyspnoea, tachypnoea and rales. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation with reciprocal depression and chest radiography showed pulmonary oedema signs. Coronary angiography showed no significant lesions, followed by ventricular tachycardia and cardiac arrest.

Echocardiography showed a calcified bioprosthesis with critical stenosis and thrombosis. Emergency thrombolysis was unsuccessful and cardiogenic shock with multi-organ dysfunction followed. Peripheral veno-arterial ECMO was started as a bridge, with a vascular injury at femoral cannulation requiring external iliac artery exposure and repair, and a redo aortic valve replacement with a mechanical valve was performed after VA-ECMO support.

Cardiac function improved, but persistent respiratory failure from ventilator-associated pneumonia required conversion to VV-ECMO. After de-cannulation he was discharged for outpatient management. Telephone follow-up about 1 year after surgery found him living without complications or cardiac-related symptoms.

summary.text: A 39-year-old man had severe mitral insufficiency from papillary muscle rupture treated with a mechanical mitral valve replacement, then a prolonged ICU stay with bacteraemia treatment. Three months later he developed bacterial endocarditis of the prosthesis and had a second replacement with a 31 mm mechanical valve.

Ten months later he presented with orthopnoea, oedema, hypotension and oliguria. Transoesophageal echocardiography showed mitral regurgitation from prosthetic ring dehiscence, with cardiogenic shock and pulmonary oedema. Planned pre-operative VA-ECMO was not used because of rapid deterioration; cardiopulmonary bypass via femoral cut-down was used, a third redo mitral valve replacement was done, and VA-ECMO was then started.

He was de-cannulated and discharged, and received 6 additional weeks of outpatient antibiotic treatment. At follow-up about 1 year after surgery, the second patient was reported to have died in the subsequent year due to new valvular complications.

summary.text: A 21-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic fever and a bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement in 2015 presented with dyspnoea, orthopnoea and fatigue, with signs of congestion and hypoperfusion. Echocardiography showed critical stenosis of the bioprosthetic mitral valve and pulmonary thromboembolism was diagnosed.

A decision was made for thrombolysis with transient improvement; cardiogenic shock and multi-organ dysfunction developed 48 h later. VA-ECMO was used as a bridge to surgery, and a redo mitral valve replacement with a 25 mm mechanical valve was then performed during that support.

After de-cannulation she developed Klebsiella pneumoniae septicaemia treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics for 18 days and was later discharged. At about 1 year she was living without complications or cardiac-related symptoms.
